داستان فیلم، یک زن میانسال مهاجر چینی ناراضی از زندگی را نشان می‌دهد که توسط نسخه آلفای شوهرش، برای مقابله با شیطانی که تلاش می‌کند چندجهانی را نابود کند به مقابله فراخوانده می‌شود. به جز اِولین شخصیت اصلی (البته اگر بشود چنین فیلمی را دارای شخصیت خواند)، چند شخصیت دیگر حضور دارند. ویموند، شوهرش که در آستانه طلاق از اوست. جوی، دخترش افسرده‌ و  همجنس‌گرا به تصویر کشیده شده و گونگ‌گونگ، پدرش که بعد از ازدواج او را طرد کرده، اکنون نیاز به پرستاری او دارد. شیطان اصلی هم جوجو توپاکی، نسخه آلفای جوی است که پس از تجربه‌ی همه جهان‌ها میخواهد آن را نابود کند. فیلم از چهار بخش تشکیل شده است: مقدمه‌ی دوازده دقیقه‌ای شامل رختشویی و تعامل اِولین با بقیه؛ بخش همه چیز (از دقیقه ۱۲ تا ۸۸)، از حضور در اداره مالیات تا فروپاشی ذهن اِولین (مشابه جوی)؛ بخش همه‌جا (از دقیقه ۸۸ تا ۱۳۰)، از حضور مجدد در خانه تا پذیرش و در آغوش گرفتن جوی؛ و بخش یکباره (۲ دقیقه آخر)، حضور مجدد متفاوت در اداره مالیات. روایت فیلم، ملغمه‌ای آشفته از ترکیب ژانرها، جهان‌های موازی و نسخه‌های متفاوت شخصیت‌هاست که با‌ کات‌های سریع و جلوه‌های ویژه مضحک به نمایش درآمده است. طرح‌ مسائلی مثل پوچی، مهربانی، پذیرش و ... به دم‌دستی‌ترین و مبتذل‌ترین شکل ممکن انجام شده. فیلم در چهارچوب هیچ ژانری هیچ منطق و انسجامی ندارد. مرثیه‌ای برای واپسین نفس‌های سینما؛ فیلمی بی‌سر و ته که برنده هفت اسکار شده است.

EEAAO is a movie that favours its self-indulgent ideas towards creating complexity in something that it doesn't even grasp itself, talking about its usage of multi-universes as a plateau for bland existentialism. It has a few good sequences of filmmaking and cinematography that makes it feel more memorable than what it would be without its formal ambitions. I do think a better film went lost within the approach to make this as science-fiction/fantasy as possible and how a lot of the film consists of fight-scenes that purely function upon a logic that the film itself establishes; With a lot of the science fiction elements purely being there as tools to create this absurdist fantasy with which the film wants to investigate vague questions about the (in a very patriarchal form)nuclear family, broad existence and nihilistic tendencies that it connects with the familiar existence. I feel like its own perception of lesbianism is planted to uproot a social conservativity within chinese diaspora that it only toys around with and doesn't properly examine, which by itself, if done right, could deliver more clarity to this total mess of unclear ideas that cultivate an uncomplex narrative by usage of artificial complexity(again through multi-universes). It oftentimes negates philosophical content or possibly more depthful implications from the narrative by involving emotionality and estrangement with the nuclear family that is caused by generational differences directly influenced by diasporadom.

Quando comecei o filme, a primeira sensação que tive foi a de estar assistindo a uma versão alternativa de algum filme da Marvel, principalmente uma espécie de Doutor Estranho no Multiverso da Loucura com uma abordagem diferente. Talvez por eu não estar tão acostumado a ver o conceito de multiverso sendo explorado fora do universo dos super-heróis, Tudo em Todo Lugar ao Mesmo Tempo parecia uma ótima oportunidade de enxergar essa ideia por uma perspectiva mais autoral e menos limitada pelas regras de uma franquia. E é curioso porque o conceito de multiverso aqui é muito mais amplo do que simplesmente mostrar versões alternativas dos personagens ou brincar com realidades diferentes. O filme usa essa ideia quase como uma representação das infinitas possibilidades da vida, das escolhas que fazemos e de todos os caminhos que poderiam ter sido seguidos. Essa é uma proposta interessante, e eu gostei da forma como o filme tenta enxergar o multiverso por um lado mais humano e existencial. O problema, para mim, está na forma como essa ideia é apresentada. Em muitos momentos, o filme parece querer ser mais inteligente do que realmente é, como se precisasse constantemente provar sua própria genialidade. A mistura de estilos, o exagero visual e a quantidade absurda de ideias fazem parte da identidade da obra, mas às vezes a sensação é de que o filme força tanto a sua criatividade que acaba perdendo um pouco da naturalidade. Ele quer ser caótico, profundo, engraçado e emocionante ao mesmo tempo, mas em alguns momentos parece mais preocupado em mostrar o quanto consegue ser diferente do que realmente desenvolver tudo aquilo que propõe. Eu gostei mais do ato final justamente porque é o momento em que o filme finalmente parece entender a própria força. Depois de passar boa parte da duração mergulhado em um caos constante, entre cortes frenéticos, exageros visuais e uma tentativa quase desesperada de ser irreverente, ele finalmente desacelera e permite que seus personagens existam de verdade. É quando Tudo em Todo Lugar ao Mesmo Tempo deixa de tentar provar o tempo todo o quanto é criativo e começa a explorar aquilo que realmente tinha de mais interessante: as relações humanas por trás de todo aquele espetáculo. Antes disso, porém, eu tive muita dificuldade de me conectar com a proposta. Não é pelo fato de o filme ser absurdo ou querer ser engraçado, porque essa é claramente a identidade dele, mas pela forma como ele constantemente interrompe os próprios momentos de profundidade. Sempre que surge uma oportunidade de desenvolver melhor suas ideias sobre arrependimentos, escolhas e a sensação de insignificância diante de infinitas possibilidades, o filme parece escolher quebrar a atmosfera com uma piada que muitas vezes não funciona e acaba tirando todo o peso daquilo que estava sendo construído. E isso acaba prejudicando justamente a profundidade que ele tenta alcançar. Algumas cenas são tão forçadas e constrangedoras que, ao invés de aproximarem o espectador dos personagens, criam uma distância. O filme quer ser caótico, divertido e emocionante, mas em muitos momentos o caos domina tanto que a parte humana fica escondida. Só quando ele finalmente abandona um pouco essa necessidade de transformar tudo em uma grande piada é que a mensagem começa a encontrar espaço para respirar. Eu realmente acredito que a campanha desse filme no Oscar foi um delírio coletivo. Sinceramente, não consigo enxergar uma obra digna de sete estatuetas aqui. Para mim, o único prêmio realmente justificável é o de Melhor Montagem. Todo o restante parece premiar mais a ideia do filme do que a sua execução. É uma obra que força a própria genialidade, insiste em uma profundidade que raramente alcança e, justamente quando parece prestes a dizer algo verdadeiramente significativo, escolhe sabotar o momento com um humor que, para mim, soa artificial e deslocado. E no fim, eu continuo com a sensação de que assistir a Tudo em Todo Lugar ao Mesmo Tempo não foi uma experiência tão distante de assistir a um filme da fase 4 da Marvel. Talvez exista mais criatividade na forma, uma identidade visual mais autoral e uma ambição maior nas ideias, mas a essência ainda me parece muito semelhante. O multiverso continua sendo tratado como um grande espetáculo, onde tudo precisa ser maior, mais caótico e mais excêntrico do que o anterior. Se a Academia decidiu premiar justamente esse tipo de proposta com o maior prêmio da noite, então talvez fosse mais coerente ter reconhecido um dos próprios filmes da Marvel, que, gostando ou não, sempre assumiram esse espetáculo sem a necessidade de revesti-lo com uma profundidade que, para mim, aqui nunca se concretiza.

Tudo em Todo o Lugar ao Mesmo Tempo (2022), de Daniel Kwan e Daniel Scheinert, é um filme cuja inventividade visual é inegável. A direção de arte, o uso das cores e a composição dos quadros sustentam um espetáculo imagético que raramente deixa a tela perder energia. O problema é que, conforme a narrativa avança e os conflitos centrais começam a aparecer, essa exuberância formal passa a competir com o próprio drama. Em vários momentos, o filme me lembrou um episódio estendido de Rick and Morty, insistindo o tempo inteiro em provar o quanto é "maluco" e "criativo", mas girando em torno da mesma dinâmica até ela perder o impacto. O excesso vira um fim em si mesmo, quase um exercício de estilo, e a montagem acelerada acaba produzindo uma sensação de clipe permanente. As discussões sobre família, identidade e aceitação existem, mas parecem sempre mediadas pelo humor e pelo absurdo, como se o filme não confiasse que essas ideias conseguiriam se sustentar sem um novo estímulo a cada poucos segundos. Isso enfraquece a construção psicológica dos personagens: muitas mudanças simplesmente acontecem, sem que a mise-en-scène ou o roteiro construam um percurso emocional convincente até elas. Went in with zero expectations. Didn't need logic, didn't need deep character work — just wanted something genuinely fun and entertaining. And honestly, I just ended up bored. The whole “genre-blending” thing isn't as wild as people say. Sure, it jumps between worlds and tosses in sci-fi, action, and some emotional moments, but none of it ever actually blends into something fresh or mind-blowing. It's just a movie that changes costumes without ever becoming genuinely entertaining. The multiverse stuff, which is supposed to be the big selling point, got repetitive fast. They create a couple of cool, weird worlds early on, but then keep revisiting the same handful over and over. “Everything Everywhere All at Once” quickly shrinks into “a few things, a few places”. That killed the sense of endless possibility and just made it feel small and monotonous. Also, people praise the relentless pace, but I honestly didn't feel it. The editing is busy, not fast — there's a difference. Especially the last hour dragged like crazy. So many slow-motion moments that didn't earn their weight, stretching out scenes that already felt emotionally repetitive. And the humor? The problem isn't that the jokes are random or dumb — it's that the movie never commits to real chaos. It gives you a couple of weird ideas, then just keeps circling back to them until they're completely worn out. A truly random, limitless multiverse should be throwing something new at you constantly, but instead the jokes become predictable, cliché, and as limited as the worlds themselves. That's really the core issue here: the movie runs out of ideas and then just stretches everything thin, repeating itself because it doesn't know what else to do. If you're going to be this narratively limited, you'd better have deep characters, sharp logic, or some real emotional weight to fall back on — and it has none of that. The emotional beats are so forced, practically holding up cue cards that say “care now” and “cry here”. Given how wild and limitless the premise is, the ending lands as preachy, cliché, and a total drag — exactly the kind of safe landing a film like this should have avoided. Honestly, it's not that different from plenty of other weak films that start with a decent premise and then fumble it. The only difference is this one got a sky-high rating and a pile of Oscars.

I also found some of the themes and relationships in the film unnecessary and distracting rather than meaningful. In the end, this is only my personal opinion, but out of respect for my love of cinema and the films that truly leave a lasting impact, I have to say that this one simply didn’t work for me. I’m glad I watched this film. It’s been on my watchlist for a very long time. It seems like it’s a bit of a love-it-or-hate-it kind of film, and I wasn’t expecting to land in the middle on it. But that’s what happened. I wasn’t disappointed, but I definitely wasn’t blown away. Okay, that’s a lie — I was blown away for parts of it, but I was checked out for other parts. This movie is beautifully shot, competently written, and there is very obvious artistic intent and passion that comes across in every scene. Even if I hated every second of it, which I didn’t, I would have to admire the sheer ambition and creativity that’s on display here. But ultimately the takeaway seems to be “everything is absurd, but we can still find truth in the chaos, form connections, and even be inspired by others despite life’s meaninglessness,” and to me, that’s just not a unique enough sentiment to warrant such a unique film. It was also just a bit heavy-handed in the way it was conveyed. There definitely wasn’t any room for interpretation. Everything Everywhere All At Once was clearly a passion project for everyone involved. I’m sure in the end they made the film they set out to make, and are very happy with the finished product. Obviously this film has an audience, and I wish I could say I’m a big fan, because good golly was this movie an experience, but sadly it left me feeling underwhelmed when the credits rolled. It ultimately amounted to spectacle — packaged as avant-garde but somehow failing to tap into something universal, which is ironic given the title. Then, I suppose this film is for everything, everywhere, but not necessarily every one .

Everything… shares the same theme as both Encanto and Turning Red and considering it’s a movie for adults, lands pretty much at the same place, with somehow less grace and sophistication. Let’s start with the rock bit - it’s been done already in I Heart Huckabees with less google eyes. Additionally, like many other LB reviewers, it’s hard not to see some heavy lifting from the most notorious episode of Rick and Morty . Do I even need to highlight recent movies about generational trauma or multiverses? Truly, other than the throw everything at the wall visuals, Everything… generates no new thematic or intellectual ideas whatsoever - the universe is large, be nice to your kids, it’s all about love, zzz. None of these would be bad on their face if they were inferred through the story - but most of them are dumped as platitudes in the final exhausting 30 minutes. The word “messy” keeps coming up in reviews as an almost compliment. I thought I'd be in the tank for this, and there's a banger of a 90 minute film trapped in here, but it's definitely from the team that brought you Swiss Army Man, and I think that should tell you everything you need to know, even if fanny-pack kung fu replaces a farting corpse. (Although not quite: unlike that film, this one is laden in exposition of its multiverse concept, one we haven't seen in a film since, like, December.) I am glad I saw it on the big screen (thanks for hosting, Letterboxd, don't hate me!) and there are real laughs, some terrific performances, one scene I consider absolutely a top ten of the year contender (I'll call it "a planet that failed to produce life") and a few great set pieces. And just even figuring out how this took less than a year to shoot staggers the brain. But it's emotional maximalism that fails to even stir me as it gets lost in whatever through line it's trying to cling onto, only to spend minutes of exposition in that through line telling us what to feel about this or that aspect. To paraphrase Lao Tzu: more stuff means less.

I'm 26 and feel like one of the definitive psychological features of my existence is the sense of looming, sinister omniscience thrust upon me and my peers by all the ways the world is now so connected and accessible, but specifically the internet, coupled with a theoretical omnipotence born of Western bootstrappy individualism. I assume that such feelings are not unique to the internet generation but they must be at least amped up? At any moment I can pull out my phone and see any kind of porn I can imagine, videos of cartel murders, endless wikipedia wormholes, torrented academic journals, highlight reels of the lives of friends and acquaintances and celebrities, instantaneous communication with all of them theoretically possible. Obviously the idea that *everything* is on the internet (or TV, or even in books) is a malicious fallacy, but it's close enough for the effect to be total. The endless possibilities and contradictions of the world are not just at my fingertips but always humming in the back of my mind. And on top of that I am told that I could have any of these experiences, be any of these people, if only I set that goal and applied myself. YMMV with that sense of monumentally unrealized infinite potential, I'm a middle-class cis(?) [edit: nope] white guy(?) [edit: nope] so maybe not everyone is brought up in such a way that "you can do anything you set your mind to" is such a deadening, constant pressure, but even with the differences in what kind of privilege individuals are born into, I think it's fairly safe to say that idea undergirds the psychology of the West. My point is - Richard Brody is bar none my favorite film critic and I was delighted to read his pan of this extremely mixed bag, this high-exertion simulation of an imaginative or ambitious movie, but I can't quite bring myself to agree that it's fundamentally cynical. I think it's bewildering that there is not more—much more—media concerned with what a soul-winnowing mindfuck the internet era is. And the story the Daniels are trying to tell here—of a boomer having to understand and experience the postmodern nihilism of her gen-z daughter in order to pull her back from the edge, and more deeply accept the merits of her own disappointing life in the process—is sweet, timely, and appreciated. I think it's a nice story with a broad understanding of one of the central pains or dilemmas of modern life. And that pushes me over the edge into generally liking this movie despite my misgivings. The misgivings: it is an earnest film but not a sincere one. Anything truly sincere will necessarily be more probing and reflective than this incurious, prefabricated roller coaster of platitudes, which constantly points to the Daniels' background in commercials and music videos not as artists but corporate propagandists of sentiment (that phrasing sounds extreme but I mean it as differentiation more than condemnation). It's garbled and constrictive, the weight of its relationships shredded by its striving for complete universality, and by, as Brody notes, every supporting character existing as a single problem for Michelle Yeoh to solve with kindness. Sweetie husband, bitter IRS agent, conservative dad, postmodern daughter. Little dimensionality. The building blocks of this film are sentiment and nonsense. "Nonsense" in that all of the film's lo-fi expository fantasy and zany humor (rarely funny) exists in a vacuum, and the Daniels—gimmick directors with some technical skill and ostensible bravura but little sense of texture or poetry—refuse to milk it, to make it evocative or dramatic, to provide variety. That is, they have little investment in the ramifications of their fantasy world and milquetoast absurdism, and it's all simply a dazzling (in the sense of being psychically blinding) package for the threadbare trail of stock reassurances they've carefully laid out. A fresh coat of paint applied via jackhammer. Again, I think what they're trying to address with this film is worthy; how they resolve it, less so. It is at its best and worst in the MILD SPOILERS I GUESS rock scene, one of the only times—in fact, THE only time—the Daniels employ their hyperactive multiverse conceit for any kind of distinct textural effect, but also the scene where the film's most unrelentingly direct and trite sentiments are emphatically laid out as text onscreen, feeling for all the world like a facebook-viral photoshopped screenshot of an inspirational message exchange. And I find the idea of that scene, uh, poignant to say the least, you have NO idea how often, when I'm depressed, I imagine myself having been born as a rock, existing in awed, wondrous jealousy of any form of life at all, let alone one as complex as humanity. I have no segue out of this paragraph, just wanted to mention that scene, the film's apex and nadir. Proof there's such a thing as an enormous quantity of very little at all. Endless reviews being like "it is what it says on the tin" but there's a lot less going on here than it appears on the surface. It is also rarely funny (Jenny Slate wyd???? Tf???); pretty dull-looking with unimaginative, even arbitrary and thoughtless compositions and mise en scene (most of the movie is set in the IRS building and it is a massive failure of production design and direction, a symbolically key location that dominates 75% of a 140-minute movie and conveys nothing, not even an intentional sense of Kafkaesque anonymity or blandness, it's totally inexpressive - another example of the Daniels' disinterest in plumbing the implications and possibilities of any element of their film beyond their narrow chain of preordained emotional beats and hackneyed gags). Michelle Yeoh, Ke Huy Quan, and Stephanie Hsu - all absolutely terrific. They're all so good, so charming, so convincing in their depth of feeling, I wish they were in a better movie. Good turn from Jamie Lee Curtis too. Also loved the raccoon puppet. Final note: my packed Thursday-night IMAX theater crowd fucking ATE this up, never have I seen a movie and immediately suspected half the audience was gonna walk out with this as one of their new favorite movies. I don't really think this is going to happen, I dunno, but I wouldn't be remotely surprised if this is a serious Oscar contender next year, even a Best Picture contender. I suspect this film will stay in the conversation for the rest of the year, it's gonna get so much hate and so much love, backlash and backlash to the backlash etc. Last night I opened up letterboxd and flipped through recent reviews and the flood of 5-stars and people calling it one of their favorite movies was exactly what I expected. So many people are going to looooove love love this movie. And I say that with (almost) no judgment. Will be interesting and probably exhausting to see how its phenomenon grows

This movie already exists and it's called The Matrix Evelyn Wang (Michelle Yeoh) leads a boring life. She runs a failing laundromat with her meek husband Waymond (Jonathan Ke Quan) and fusses over her directionless, standoffish daughter Joy (Stephanie Hsu). During a meeting with IRS agent Deidre (Jamie Lee Curtis), Waymond suddenly changes, informing her that he is a version of her husband from an alternate universe and that she is the only one who can save the multiverse from an ultimate destructive force. If you've seen a sci-fi movie made in the last 20 years, then multiverses, body-swapping, and all the mumbo-jumbo those things entail will be pretty easy for you to understand. Unfortunately, the filmmakers don't think so. The Daniels' first film, Swiss Army Man is so comfortable not explaining itself. It presents the audience with a farting boner corpse whose body can be used in a myriad useful ways for wilderness survival, and it never takes a second to explain how all of it works. Because it doesn't need to. All of the people who complain about Christopher Nolan's films having too much exposition are going to love this, even though this movie is almost entirely explaining things that are already pretty clear. There is so much to love here: The Daniel's have a wonderful, kinetic visual style, Michelle Yeoh and Stephanie Hsu give fantastically funny and compelling performances, the action is uniformly fun and exciting (although not groundbreaking or physically impressive), and pretty much all of the jokes work. The alternate universe stuff is all really good. Almost all of them are basically one-note gags, but The Daniels' have a really good handle on how to draw emotion out of a world where people have frankfurters for fingers, or extended riffs on Ratatouille and the works of Wong Kar-wai. Once the movie is allowed to actually get going, there is so much to enjoy. If this was 20 minutes shorter and didn't treat its audience like slop drinking fools, it would pretty easily be one of my favourites of the year.

Multiverses are so hot right now. And why shouldn’t they be? At a time when people can’t even look at their phones without being confronted by a seemingly infinite number of competing realities — a time which everything seems close enough to touch, but almost nothing feels possible to change, and even the happiest people you know are haunted by the endless possibilities of who else they might have been — telling a story that only takes place on a single plane of existence might as well be an act of denial. That isn’t a problem for the filmmaking duo of Daniel Kwan and Daniel Scheinert (better known as Daniels), who once created an interactive six-minute short that could be played in 3,618,502,788,666,131,106,986,593,281,521,497,120,414,687,020,801,267,626, 233,049,500,247,285,301,248 different ways. These guys aren’t just uniquely prepared to meet the present moment, they’ve been waiting for it to catch up with them for a long time. So it’s not much of a surprise that the project they’ve been working on since 2016’s “Swiss Army Man” sees the crisis of living with “Everything Everywhere All at Once” more clearly than any other movie like it. Not that there are any other movies like it. Here is an orgiastic work of slaphappy genius that doesn’t operate like a narrative film so much as a particle accelerator — or maybe a cosmic washing machine — that two psychotic 12-year-olds designed in the hopes of reconciling the anxiety of what our lives could be with the beauty of what they are. It’s a machine powered by the greatest performance that Michelle Yeoh has ever given, pumped full of the zaniest martial arts battles that Stephen Chow has never shot, and soaked through with the kind of “anything goes” spirit that’s only supposed to be on TV these days. “Everything Everywhere All at Once” is as overstuffed as its title implies, even more juvenile than its pedigree suggests, and so creatively unbound from the minute it starts that it makes Daniels’ previous efforts seem like they were made with Bressonian restraint by comparison (for context, their last feature was a sweet fable starring Harry Potter as an explosively farting corpse). It’s a movie that I saw twice just to make sure I hadn’t completely hallucinated it the first time around, and one that I will soon be seeing a third time for the same reason. I don’t ever expect to understand how it was (or got) made, but I already know that it works. And I know that it works because my impulse to pick on its imperfections and wonder how it might’ve been different eventually forfeits to the utter miracle of its existence. ~this review continues on IndieWire~

This movie on paper should not have worked as well as it did. A multiverse Kung Fu movie, with an absurd and silly premise, but man oh man was this just the most screwball, incredible, absurd in the best way, mindfuck of a life affirming masterpiece. This is a brilliant and heartwarming refutation of nihilism, and the single most unique film I've ever seen. Each of the core cast members is delightful, and looking like they had the time of their life making this bonkers ass film. Special consideration though goes to Ke Huy Quan and Michelle Yeoh as the anchors of the film, especially Michelle Yo. They are called on to do it all, playing dozens of absurd multiversal versions of themselves, the action, and the hard hitting powerful emotion and they both deliver it and then some. Stephanie Hsu, and Jamie Lee Curtis are also delightful in their roles and more limited screentime. But the things I want to highlight most about this film are the direction, editing, and screenplay. A movie like this would be so so easy to screw up. Too confusing, too messy, too crammed. But Daniels strike the perfect balance here with a wonderfully tight, heartfelt, creative, and bonkers screenplay, pared with immensely creative direction. Just some wonderful camerawork here both from the emotional moments, as well as the insanely fun action sequences. But the MVP for me is the editing. Paul Rogers the editor here, in collaboration with the directors took something nigh incomprehensible, and turned it into the most creative, fun, acid trip to your senses delight I've maybe ever seen, while keeping it still easy to follow and track with. This is no easy feat, and it was a masterclass on display. If this doesn't win best editing at next year's Academy Awards I will find and hurt someone. All in all I can only do so much to describe this film. It's the kind of thing you can only understand by experiencing yourself. This is must see on a big screen, and must see period. I would be shocked if many films, if any top this for me in the remainder of 2022. Well done to every member of the cast and crew here. This is the best, most thought provoking action film since the original Matrix and I am ALIVE.
